title: A Pore That Pays for Potassium

scenes.tts: A potassium channel can pass up to about a hundred million potassium ions a second. Yet for every thousand potassium ions, fewer than one sodium ion gets through. Sodium is the smaller ion. Its radius is zero point nine five angstroms, against one point three three for potassium. So the pore cannot be a simple sieve.
scenes.caption: A potassium channel can pass up to about a hundred million potassium ions a second. Yet for every thousand potassium ions, fewer than one sodium ion gets through. Sodium is the smaller ion. Its radius is 0.95 Å, against 1.33 Å for potassium. So the pore cannot be a simple sieve.
scenes.visual: Schematic channel: a stream of potassium discs runs through while sodium discs are turned away at the top. Chips give the two rates. Then a sodium disc and a larger potassium disc side by side with their radii, and a crossed-out simple sieve chip.
scenes.narration: A potassium channel can pass up to about a hundred million potassium ions a second. Yet for every thousand potassium ions, fewer than one sodium ion gets through. Sodium is the smaller ion. Its radius is 0.95 Å, against 1.33 Å for potassium. So the pore cannot be a simple sieve.

scenes.tts: Think of it as a trade. In water, every ion wears a coat of water molecules, and stripping that coat costs energy. An ion will enter a narrow pore only if the pore pays the cost back. In nineteen ninety-eight, Roderick MacKinnon's laboratory showed how, with the structure of K C S A, a potassium channel from a soil bacterium.

scenes.visual: A potassium disc with a dashed water coat above the channel. The coat strips away and a red cost bar grows; the disc waits at the narrow entrance until a green pay-back bar grows to meet it. Then the bars clear and a chip names MacKinnon, 1998 and KcsA.
scenes.narration: Think of it as a trade. In water, every ion wears a coat of water molecules, and stripping that coat costs energy. scenes.tts: Four identical subunits surround one pore. Near the outer end it narrows to a selectivity filter, twelve angstroms long, too tight for an ion to keep its water. The filter is lined with carbonyl oxygen atoms from the protein's backbone, set in rings that surround a potassium ion much as the oxygens of water did. Potassium swaps water for protein and loses almost nothing.

scenes.visual: The channel with a chip for four identical subunits around one pore. A bracket marks the filter, 12 Å long. A potassium disc loses its coat at the entrance, the purple oxygen lining appears, and the disc slides in snug against it. Cost and pay-back bars come out nearly equal.
scenes.narration: Four identical subunits surround one pore. Near the outer end it narrows to a selectivity filter, 12 Å long, too tight for an ion to keep its water. The filter is lined with carbonyl oxygen atoms from the protein's backbone, set in rings that surround a potassium ion much as the oxygens of water did. Potassium swaps water for protein and loses almost nothing.

scenes.tts: Sodium is too small to touch all the oxygens of a ring at once, and in the nineteen ninety-eight account the filter is held too stiffly to close in on it. For sodium, leaving water costs more than the filter repays, so it stays outside. Two potassium ions sit in the filter in single file, and the repulsion between them pushes one out as the next arrives. That is the answer for potassium channels; sodium and calcium channels build their filters differently.

scenes.visual: A sodium disc in the filter with gaps to the lining on both sides and a note that the lining stays put. The cost bar is long and the pay-back bar short, and the sodium disc is sent back out. Then two potassium discs in single file, a third arrives, repulsion arrows, and the lower one leaves. A final chip says other channels differ.
